Coming back from @aiDotEngineer Code in San Francisco, I realized how much the AI Engineer profession has changed in just one year. It's wild.

A few cool talks helped me see the bigger picture.
When agents can write, run, and fix code on their own, what does the AI engineer do?

1. @simonw (interview dropping this week!) noted that GPT-5.1 and Claude Opus 4.5 made daily autonomous coding real. So engineers got freedom to move to other tasks, but the new challenge is handling all the small, unspoken decisions.

2. @lydiahallie, who works on Claude Code at Anthropic, showed how agents miss edge cases like keeping active users logged in during an auth update. The job shifts to spotting hidden assumptions, turning them into tests, and managing dozens of parallel sessions.

3. @poteto (Lauren Tan) shared how her team shipped 11,000 changes to Grok Bot in October while making it faster. The real work took ~6 months beforehand: encoding engineering experience into system checks so agents stop repeating the same bad shortcuts.

4. @Steve_Yegge proved that coding speed stops being the bottleneck. In his game Wyvern, agents shipped features so fast that players asked him to slow down and publish a roadmap just to keep up.

I packed many more insights, including the ones from Thariq Shihipar's talk, into this video to capture this new wave in AI engineering. Watch my full AIE Code overview here or on Youtube:

How to fit an open model to YOUR coding agent. Super concrete recipe from @ClementDelangue and the @huggingface team, who took @Alibaba_Qwen's Qwen3.8-27B from 39% to 65% on SWE-bench Pro (hard 51) with RL and one small LoRA:

1. Keep the harness, adapt the model.
The same model behaves differently in different harnesses. Each one has its own tools, prompt and control flow. So instead of switching harnesses to get a better model, they train a small LoRA adapter per harness and you swap it in behind the agent you already use. First one is for @pidotdev.

2. Train inside the real, unmodified harness.
The harness runs as is, in its own sandbox per rollout, and training uses exactly the tokens the harness saw. No re-tokenisation, no simplified copy of the agent.

3. Reward correctness, then efficiency.
The reward is the task verifier's correctness plus a tool-efficiency bonus with weight 0.1. Tasks: 750 scale800 tasks mixed with 300 TermGrade tasks, 8 rollouts per task.

4. Keep the adapter small.
LoRA r = 32, alpha = 64, on the attention and MLP projections. Async GRPO in TRL, learning rate 2e-5, 2× B200 per harness. The released checkpoint is step 160. The run was stopped at step 191 of 1,000 planned.

5. Block reward hacking during training.
A proxy called safeagents checks every tool call. Clear attempts to hack the reward are blocked and score 0. In an earlier ablation, turning the guard on changed accuracy by +0.0 ± 4.1 points. It costs nothing.

6. Keep thinking off.
With thinking off, the adapter matches the base model at its highest reasoning effort: 64.7% vs 64.7% on SWE-bench Pro, 56.6% vs 54.2% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, with about 4.5× fewer tokens. Turning thinking on for the adapter adds nothing.

7. Check your evals before you celebrate.
The first version of the model card said 29.4% → 62.7%. Then they found nine base-model runs had failed because the tunnel between the sandboxes and the model server went down. They reran the affected runs on both sides: 39.2% → 64.7%. Smaller jump, still +25.5 points, 15 tasks newly solved vs 2 lost.

The results they report under pi: SWE-bench Pro (hard 51) 39.2% → 64.7%, Terminal-Bench 2.1 39.5% → 55.8%, and less than half the turns on the tasks both models solve (23 vs 59 median on SWE-bench Pro). Apache 2.0, open weights, a GGUF version for llama.cpp, and an @opencode adapter came out today.

And what about "just use a bigger model"?

The interesting thing is that the harness itself becomes training data. You can't do this with a closed model. With an open one, a 27B model you run locally gets fitted to the tools you actually use.

With all this raw intelligence, we need to dumb down how users actually choose and operate these models.

8 models graded 620 anonymized medical answers. Every one of them ranked its own answer higher than the other 7 judges did. About 1.2 places on average, almost 3 for GPT-5.6 Sol. Telling them which model wrote which answer barely changed it.

A lot of the leaderboards we read every week use a single LLM judge. How many of those results would hold up with a judge from a different model family?

Looped Transformers are low-key fascinating. First of all, you need to understand what travels around the loop and the 3 core things you set for the architecture.

A Looped Transformer runs the same Transformer block (or stack) for multiple passes, feeding each output back in as the next input.

▪️ What travels around this loop is the hidden state:

- Token embeddings form the initial hidden representation.
- The shared stack updates that representation via attention and feed-forward operations.
- Its output goes back to the stack for another pass, using an updated hidden state. Some designs also reuse the input, add time-step embeddings, or run multiple residual streams.
- After the chosen number of passes, the output head converts the selected representation into token scores.

That's all to win additional computation without an additional set of block weights for every pass.

Although the weights stay the same during inference, changing inputs let the same block produce different updates. During decoding it attends via the KV cache, during prefill it updates masked tokens in parallel.

A model can loop its entire stack or repeat only a middle stack between ordinary input and output blocks.
Note that repeating the stack doesn't require generating a new text token between passes.

▪️ So there are 3 basic things you need to identify for the specific Looped Transformer architecture:

1. The repeated blocks
2. The state they receive
3. The rule that controls their execution - a fixed number of passes, a user-selected count, or an adaptive rule

Lots of self-improving agent papers this week. A good chunk of the gains turn out to be agents getting better at the benchmark, not the task. So we put the papers that actually check first.

1. Beneath the Surface: What We Overlook When We Talk About Agent Evolution
Evolving the harness can lift benchmark scores with no weight updates, but the gains are unreliable, expensive and transfer poorly. Read this one first.

2. Learning the Task or Learning the Verifier?
Show a self-improving embodied coding agent the benchmark's success criteria and its score goes up. Its actual task completion doesn't.

3. Evidence-Governed Adoption of Self-Generated Updates in Autonomous AI Agents
Separates "the agent wrote a change" from "the agent ships it". Every change has to pass fresh paired audits and a non-inferiority check first.

4. Harness^2: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World
A harness that improves itself on new tasks without an answer key, by test-running edits and keeping what helps.

5. Experience-Handoff Reinforcement Learning for Recursive Self-Improvement
Agents trained with RL learn to write and curate notes for their future runs, not only to pick better actions.

6. InfraRSI: Harnessing Recursive Self-Improvement for Training Infrastructure
Self-improvement where it's hardest: distributed training, where one bad edit means an OOM or silent numerical drift. Every optimization gets verified.

7. Incentivizing Self-Learning in Large Language Models via Reinforcement Learning
Give a model long reference material and train it to look things up and study while it solves the problem, instead of relying on what it already knows.

8. PhysLoop: Harnessing LLMs' Physics Awareness for Self-Improving Video Generation Models
An LLM spots physics mistakes in generated videos and guides the fixes, so the video model improves on cleaner data.

9. A Cross-Scenario Survey and Analysis of Self-Evolving Multimodal Agents
Why a self-improvement trick that works for reasoning often breaks for navigation or manipulation. A good map of the field.
